title: London police officer convicted in woman's custody death appeals again
subtitle: A London police officer convicted of failing to provide the necessaries of life in the 2016 custody death of an Indigenous woman has appealed the conviction - again.
article: A London police officer convicted of failing to provide the necessaries of life in the 2016 custody death of an Indigenous woman has appealed the conviction - again.
Last month, Const. Nicholas Doering was given an 18-month conditional sentence last month for his role in the Sept. 6, 2016, death of Debra Chrisjohn, 39, a mother of 11.
Chrisjohn's sister Cindy called the latest appeal "ridiculous" and said she fears Doering's conviction will be overturned and he'll keep his job.
"Convicted and sentenced twice. Makes no sense to me for him to be still running free," Cindy Chrisjohn said in an online message Monday.

Doering was initially given a 12-month jail sentence in 2020 after he was of convicted of criminal negligence causing death and failing to provide the necessaries of life, but the Ontario Court of Appeal overturned the criminal negligence conviction last year and ordered a resentencing.

Now, one month after Superior Court Regional Senior Justice Renee Pomerance imposed the conditional sentence , half of which Doering will spend on house arrest, he has launched an appeal, his lawyer Alan Gold confirmed Monday.

Doering is entitled to appeal his sentence because the first appeal led to an acquittal on the criminal negligence causing death charge and the failing to provide the necessaries of life was set aside before Pomerance ultimately convicted Doering of the charge, making it a new conviction, Gold said.
Gold filed a notice of appeal asking the Ontario Court of Appeal to acquit Doering, stay the charge or order a new trial.

Doering's defence will argue Pomerance had no jurisdiction to consider the application to reopen proceedings in the failure to provide the necessaries of life charge, according to a notice to appeal filed last month.
Other arguments will centre on Doering's interactions with police and paramedics, the document says.

Doering falsely told OPP officers that Chrisjohn, whom he had arrested in east London after she was found walking into traffic while high on crystal methamphetamine, had been medically assessed by paramedics, court heard.

But Doering was relying on a conversation with Middlesex-London EMS supervisor Sean Hill, who looked at Chrisjohn through a police cruiser window after her arrest, and told Doering her vitals would be "out of whack due to the drug" and he could take her to the hospital, but would end up waiting for hours while she was monitored, court heard.

"A negligent omission that is not alleged to be a criminal cause of a subsequent death cannot logically be alleged to be a criminal endangerment to that same life," the notice of appeal says. "This issue only requires consideration after the criminal negligence causing death conviction is set aside."
The Appeal Court will schedule a hearing before a panel of three judges after all of the filings in the case have been completed.

Doering has been suspended with pay since he was sentenced on Sept. 21, 2020, and was taken briefly into custody before being granted bail after his first appeal was filed. Police chiefs in Ontario have no authority to withhold salaries from suspended officers, unless they're convicted of a criminal offence and sentenced to jail.

Once his criminal case is completed, Doering will face an investigation under the Police Services Act, the law governing policing in Ontario, under which police forces hold disciplinary hearings into professional misconduct.
